transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, what brings me in is... I've just been living with this constant mix of guilt, fear, and anger since my friend was killed. It's just heavy, you know? And it hasn't eased up the way everyone seemed to think it would. They all said, "Oh, time heals all wounds," but I don't know who made that up. Probably someone who never had to deal with anything real. Speaking of time, I was trying to organize my garden the other day—I have these beautiful hydrangeas, the blue ones, not the pink. I read somewhere that the soil acidity changes the color, which is fascinating, really. I spent hours reading about soil pH instead of actually gardening. But anyway, yeah, the anger and the guilt... it's just always there.
Can you tell me more about your friend's death? Were you directly involved or present when it happened?

I... well, I don't really want to get into the exact details of that day. It's just too much to picture right now. Was I there? I... it happened over by the old downtown district. You know, they've been trying to revitalize that whole neighborhood for years now. When I first got my degree—oh, ages ago—I used to work right near that intersection. It was so bustling back then. We had this little bakery we'd go to on lunch breaks, they made the most incredible almond croissants. 

I actually tried baking them once since I retired and have all this time on my hands, but laminating dough is just... well, it’s an absolute nightmare. The butter has to be the exact right temperature. If it gets too warm, it just oozes everywhere and ruins the pastry layers. I spent a whole Tuesday scrubbing burnt butter out of the bottom of my oven. It smelled like a campfire in my kitchen for weeks. 

But... I'm sorry, what was the question? The whole thing with my friend is just... it's just a terrible mess in my head, I can't really sort out the details for you.
Do you find yourself having unwanted, intrusive memories or images of your friend’s death that come up when you don’t want them to?

Yes, unfortunately. It's... it's like I have no control over it. A crosswalk signal changing, the growl of a big truck down the street, or even just seeing one of those walking-tour maps they hand out to tourists... it just suddenly puts the whole scene right back in my head. So sharply. I can see her stepping off the curb before I can even try to stop the memory. 

It's awful, really. Speaking of tourists, though, they've completely taken over the waterfront lately. I went down there last weekend just to get some fresh air, maybe feed the gulls, and I couldn't even find a place to sit. Everyone is always looking at their phones, taking pictures of their food. I saw a young man drop an entire ice cream cone—pistachio, I think, it was very green—right onto his shoes because he was trying to take a selfie. Pistachio is such an underrated flavor, don't you think? I used to make a pistachio pound cake for the neighborhood block parties back in the nineties. I haven't made it in years, though. The price of nuts has just gone through the roof. I saw a small bag of walnuts at the grocery store for nine dollars! Nine! But yes, those images of her... they just pop up out of nowhere.
Do you find yourself avoiding places, people, or activities that remind you of your friend's death?

Yes, I do. I mean, I absolutely go out of my way to avoid that intersection now. I won't even drive within a five-block radius of it. And I used to be so involved in the community, you know, but I've stopped signing up for most of the neighborhood walking tours or even the local traffic safety meetings. I just... I cannot bear the conversations because they always seem to circle back to what happened there, or to pedestrian accidents in general. 

Speaking of traffic, though, have you noticed how they changed the timing on the lights over by the new shopping center? It's completely ridiculous. You sit there for a full three minutes just waiting to turn left, and there's not a single car coming the other way! I sat there on Tuesday—or was it Wednesday? No, Tuesday, because I was on my way to the pharmacy to pick up my vitamins. I take this wonderful D3 supplement now, the gel caps, not the chalky tablets. The tablets always upset my stomach. My neighbor, Susan, she swears by the liquid drops, but I just can't get past the oily texture. She puts them in her morning tea, which sounds dreadful. Tea should just be tea, maybe a little lemon. Earl Grey is my favorite, the bergamot smells so lovely. I tried growing a bergamot plant once, but the aphids got to it before it even had a chance. Aphids are such a menace. I tried spraying them with soapy water, which is what the lady at the nursery suggested, but... oh, I'm sorry, I'm rambling again. What were we talking about? Oh, right, the intersection. Yes, I just stay far away from it now.
Have you noticed yourself losing interest in things you used to care about or enjoy, like hobbies, social activities, or other parts of your routine?

Well... yes, I suppose I have. It's strange, really. I used to be so busy. I'd spend hours planning out my garden beds every spring, and I'd quilt with the ladies at the community center on Thursdays. We'd organize these lovely theater outings, and I was always the one happily arguing at our book club meetings. But now... I just look at those things on the calendar and I feel almost nothing. It's like they belong to someone I used to be. 

Speaking of the book club, they chose a historical fiction novel this month, something about the French Revolution. I used to love historical fiction, but honestly, the covers they put on books these days are just so garish. Have you noticed that? It's all bright, blocky letters and neon colors. I miss the days when a book cover was a beautiful illustration. I have this old copy of *Pride and Prejudice* that belonged to my mother, and the cover is this delicate watercolor. It's just exquisite. I actually tried watercolor painting myself a few years ago. I thought it would be relaxing, but the paper gets all warped if you use too much water, and trying to stretch the paper beforehand is such a hassle. You have to soak it and tape it down with that special gummed tape, and half the time the tape doesn't even stick properly, and then the edges curl up anyway. I ended up with a lot of very lumpy paintings of flowers. I think I finally just gave the whole set of paints to my niece. She's quite artistic, actually. She just started college for graphic design. Or was it interior design? I can never remember. But anyway, yes, the things I used to enjoy just don't seem to hold any appeal for me anymore. I just can't seem to muster the energy for them.
Have you been feeling down or losing pleasure in most activities for most of the day, nearly every day?

Well, I wouldn't say I feel down all day, every day. It's more of a... a dullness, I suppose. I don't wake up crying or anything like that. But I just don't have that spark I used to have. 

Speaking of sparks, my neighbor finally got his old Ford Mustang running again. He's been tinkering with that car in his driveway for, oh, it must be three years now. It's a beautiful cherry red, but the noise it makes when he revs the engine! It rattles my front windows. He says he's going to take it to the classic car show over at the fairgrounds this summer. I went to that car show once, years ago, with my husband. They had the most incredible funnel cake stand. I know funnel cake is terrible for you, all that fried dough and powdered sugar, but it's just so nostalgic. You take one bite and you're ten years old again at the county fair. Although, the last time I had powdered sugar, I inhaled right as I took a bite and ended up coughing for ten minutes straight. It got all over my favorite navy blue cardigan. Navy blue is so hard to keep clean, don't you think? Every little piece of lint shows up. I have one of those sticky rollers, but the sheets never tear off cleanly. You always end up pulling off two or three at a time, which just seems so wasteful. But no, I wouldn't say I'm sad all the time. Just... flat, if that makes sense.
Have you had days where you felt this flatness or lack of interest nearly all the time, and if so, has that ever lasted for two weeks or more?

Well, no, not really. I mean, it's not like it's every single day for weeks on end. It just comes and goes, you know? Like I'll have a few days where everything just feels a bit gray, but then I'll have a decent day. 

Speaking of gray, I finally decided to repaint the guest bathroom. It was this awful mustard yellow that the previous owners chose, and I just couldn't stand it anymore. I went to the hardware store and picked out this lovely shade called "Morning Mist." It's a very soft, pale gray with just a hint of blue in it. But let me tell you, buying paint these days is an absolute ordeal. They have hundreds of little color swatches, and the lighting in the store is so fluorescent that everything looks different once you get it home. I must have bought five different sample pots before I settled on Morning Mist. And then, of course, you have to decide on the finish. Matte, eggshell, satin, semi-gloss... it's exhausting! I went with eggshell because the man at the counter said it's easier to wipe down if it gets splashed, which makes sense for a bathroom. Although, my nephew stayed over last Thanksgiving and somehow managed to get toothpaste on the ceiling. The ceiling! I still haven't figured out how he managed that. He's a lovely boy, very smart, studying engineering, but completely oblivious to his surroundings. He left his wet towel on the hardwood floor in the hallway, too. Hardwood is so sensitive to moisture. You really have to be careful with it, or it starts to warp and buckle. My cousin had to replace her entire dining room floor because of a slow leak from her radiator... but no, the flatness doesn't last for two straight weeks. It's just off and on.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight since your friend passed away?

No, I wouldn't say there have been any changes there. My clothes all still fit exactly the same, and I'm eating my usual meals. 

Although, I will say, going to the grocery store to get those meals has become such a headache lately. They completely rearranged the aisles at my local market last month. I spent twenty minutes just looking for canned tomatoes on Tuesday! Why on earth would they move the canned vegetables over by the baking supplies? It makes absolutely no sense. And speaking of baking, I wanted to make a peach cobbler because they had a big display of peaches right at the front of the store, but they were all so hard and bruised. You just can't get decent produce these days. My grandmother used to have this massive peach tree in her backyard when I was little, and the smell was just heavenly. We would sit out on her back porch and eat them right off the branch, juice dripping everywhere. You really had to watch out for the yellow jackets, though. They loved the sweet fruit just as much as we did. I actually got stung on the thumb by one when I was eight, right before my spring piano recital. My thumb swelled up like a little balloon, and I couldn't stretch my hand to play the chords properly. I was so upset, I refused to wear my new floral dress. My mother was absolutely furious with me... but anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, my appetite is perfectly fine. No weight changes or anything like that.
Have you had days where you felt down or lost pleasure in most activities for most of the day, and if so, has that ever happened nearly every day for two weeks or more?

Well, I suppose I have lost interest in things, yes. It's been going on for a while now, definitely more than two weeks. I used to plan out my garden beds every spring, you know, mapping out where the marigolds would go next to the tomatoes to keep the bugs away. And I'd quilt with the ladies on Thursdays, go to theater outings in the city, and just argue happily at my book club. We read the most fascinating biography of Eleanor Roosevelt last year. Did you know she used to hold press conferences just for female reporters because they weren't allowed into the president's press briefings? She was such a trailblazer. My aunt actually met her once, briefly, at a train station in upstate New York. My aunt was wearing this fabulous felt cloche hat with a pheasant feather—you just don't see hats like that anymore. Now everyone just wears those awful baseball caps, even indoors. It's so informal. I remember when people dressed up to fly on an airplane. My first flight was to Chicago, and I wore a tailored suit and gloves. They served an actual hot meal on real china, not just a tiny bag of pretzels that you have to tear open with your teeth. I chipped a tooth on a pretzel once, right before my niece's wedding. The dentist had to squeeze me in on a Saturday morning. He was this very young man, looked like he was barely out of high school, but he did a marvelous job matching the color of the bonding to my natural teeth. Teeth are so tricky as you get older, they just naturally yellow no matter how much you brush... but anyway, what I was saying is, now I look at those things on my calendar—the gardening, the book club—and I just feel almost nothing. It's like those activities belong to someone I used to be.

You just can't get decent produce these days. My grandmother used to have this massive peach tree in her backyard when I was little, and the smell was just heavenly. We would sit out on her back porch and eat them right off the branch, juice dripping everywhere. You really had to watch out for the yellow jackets, though. They loved the sweet fruit just as much as we did. I actually got stung on the thumb by one when I was eight, right before my spring piano recital. My thumb swelled up like a little balloon, and I couldn't stretch my hand to play the chords properly. I was so upset, I refused to wear my new floral dress. My mother was absolutely furious with me... but anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, my appetite is perfectly fine. No weight changes or anything like that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced symptoms of depression for a 2-week period, which would support a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (F33.0) over other candidates like PTSD (F43.10) or OCD (F42.9).
doctor.question: Have you had days where you felt down or lost pleasure in most activities for most of the day, and if so, has that ever happened nearly every day for two weeks or more?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to plan my garden beds, quilt with the ladies, go to theater outings, and argue happily at book club, but now I look at those things on the calendar and feel almost nothing, like they belong to someone I used to be.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about losing pleasure in most activities, which directly corresponds to the symptom of loss of interest.

patient.answer: Well, I suppose I have lost interest in things, yes. It's been going on for a while now, definitely more than two weeks. I used to plan out my garden beds every spring, you know, mapping out where the marigolds would go next to the tomatoes to keep the bugs away. And I'd quilt with the ladies on Thursdays, go to theater outings in the city, and just argue happily at my book club. We read the most fascinating biography of Eleanor Roosevelt last year. Did you know she used to hold press conferences just for female reporters because they weren't allowed into the president's press briefings? She was such a trailblazer. My aunt actually met her once, briefly, at a train station in upstate New York. My aunt was wearing this fabulous felt cloche hat with a pheasant feather—you just don't see hats like that anymore. Now everyone just wears those awful baseball caps, even indoors. It's so informal. I remember when people dressed up to fly on an airplane. My first flight was to Chicago, and I wore a tailored suit and gloves. They served an actual hot meal on real china, not just a tiny bag of pretzels that you have to tear open with your teeth. I chipped a tooth on a pretzel once, right before my niece's wedding. The dentist had to squeeze me in on a Saturday morning. He was this very young man, looked like he was barely out of high school, but he did a marvelous job matching the color of the bonding to my natural teeth. Teeth are so tricky as you get older, they just naturally yellow no matter how much you brush... but anyway, what I was saying is, now I look at those things on my calendar—the gardening, the book club—and I just feel almost nothing. It's like those activities belong to someone I used to be.

inference.note: The patient described persistent symptoms of depression, including loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities, flat affect, and intrusive memories related to trauma. However, the depressive symptoms do not meet criteria for a major depressive episode as they are not present nearly every day for at least two weeks. The primary diagnosis consistent with these findings is Adjustment Disorder with Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood (F43.10). F33.0 (Recurrent Depressive Disorder, Mild) is ruled out due to insufficient duration and severity of mood symptoms. F42.9 (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, Unspecified) is ruled out as there is no evidence of obsessions or compulsions.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent re-experiencing of a traumatic event, avoidance of trauma-related stimuli, and negative alterations in mood and interest, consistent with PTSD. The lack of persistent depressed mood or anhedonia for at least two weeks rules out major depressive disorder. Symptoms are specifically tied to the traumatic loss of a friend and do not generalize to other stressors, supporting PTSD over other stressor-related disorders.
